img_c66b2fd607cf422f.title: Beaumont High School, E. 6th Street (now Beaumont Civic Center), from the 1930 BHS yearbook
img_c66b2fd607cf422f.description: A long, single-story Mission Revival-influenced school building with a central tile-roofed gable pavilion pierced by an oculus window, flanked by banks of multi-pane classroom windows, a stepped parapet block at left, and a flag flying at right; the foreground street (E. 6th) is unpaved and the grounds are sparsely planted, consistent with recent construction. The building opened as Beaumont High School in 1928, built on Sixth Street after the demise of Magnolia High School. The scan derives from a Beaumont Library District file identifying it as the building photograph in the 1930 BHS yearbook. The school later served as a grammar school, and in the mid-1980s Beaumont City Hall relocated into it; it remains the Beaumont Civic Center at the 500 block of E. 6th Street.

img_5f9b3935055576a5.title: Beaumont School students and teachers, 1890–1893 (identified by BLD as the first Wellwood School building)
img_5f9b3935055576a5.description: Roughly seventy students of all ages, with several adult teachers among them, pose in front of a white clapboard frame schoolhouse with a large conifer at center; a bay-windowed wing stands behind the group and tall dark-trimmed windows mark the gable end at right. The mount is inscribed in period hand 'Beaumont School 1890–1893' — it does not say Wellwood. Holmes's History of Riverside County (1912) records that Beaumont's first school met in the 1884 church, that a one-room school building was erected in 1885 and later enlarged, and that by 1912 the town grammar school was called the 'Olivewood school'; the enlarged 1885 building is a plausible match for the structure shown. The Wellwood identification comes from the Beaumont Library District filename tradition ('Wellwood school old building 1890-1893'), and BLD's Calisphere records attest a pre-1921 'original Wellwood School' replaced by the 1921 building, but the name's application to this 1890s building is not confirmed by the photograph itself.

img_36bc04455099c9d7.title: Francis Dowling Jr. and son John Dowling sorting cherries, Dowling Fruit Orchards, Beaumont
img_36bc04455099c9d7.original_title: Francis Dowling Jr And Son John Dowling Sorting Cherries
img_36bc04455099c9d7.description: Color snapshot inside a packing room: an elderly Francis Dowling Jr. in a navy T-shirt and green-billed mesh cap smiles at the camera while his son John, in a white T-shirt and jeans, sorts dark cherries in a wooden bin; an orange 'WATER HEATER' sign is taped to the door at left and a box marked 'FRESH' sits at right, with customers visible in the sales room beyond. Francis Marion Dowling Jr. (Feb 13, 1925 – Oct 8, 2016) founded Dowling Fruit Orchards in 1952, planting some 25,000 trees with his father; the stand at 38021 Highway 60 in Beaumont became a local institution, with cherries among its signature crops. John Dowling (born c. 1962; aged 59 when the orchard closed in November 2021) ran the business with his wife Shelly in its final years. The catalog's former c. 1945–1958 date is impossible — it predates John's birth and nearly the business itself; the color stock, mesh-back cap, and John's apparent age as a young adult place the photograph around the 1980s to early 1990s.

img_dee5615ad57181f9.title: Laura May Stewart on her horse Pado, probably at the Stewart Ranch, 1911
img_dee5615ad57181f9.description: A small bordered snapshot, ink-inscribed 'Laura on Pado 1911', showing Laura May Stewart in a brimmed hat, work shirt, and riding trousers astride a dark saddle horse in a dirt corral; board fencing runs behind her, a farm wagon stands at left, and a windbreak of poplar or cottonwood trees rises beyond. Laura May Stewart was the daughter of Reznor Perry Stewart, who took a homestead at Beaumont in 1883 and, buying Southern Pacific land, built a 2,200-acre grain and hay ranch; Holmes (1912) records R. P. Stewart raising grain from 1884 and still resident on the ranch in 1912, making the family ranch the probable setting. The inscription's 1911 date matches two companion prints in the same BLD folder ('Laura May Stewart in chaps dated 1911' and a standing portrait). The photographer is unrecorded; the print descends through the Stewart family material held with the Beaumont Library District collection.

img_2846f7be40e9aff6.title: Horse-drawn combine harvester at work, Stewart Ranch, Beaumont area
img_2846f7be40e9aff6.description: A team of roughly two dozen horses and mules, strung out to the right, pulls a combined harvester through standing grain in a dusty field, its long header and draper frame extending to the left; at least three crew members ride the machine, and the bare foothills of the San Gorgonio Pass close the horizon. The scene belongs to the Stewart Ranch, the grain and hay operation Reznor Perry Stewart built from his 1883 Beaumont homestead — Holmes (1912) records R. P. Stewart raising grain from 1884 and still on the ranch in 1912, and the print sits in the BLD Reznor Stewart folder. Two visually distinct Calisphere prints show the same operation's harvest crews, one of them dated 1900 with Jim Barrett named as driver. Big-team combine harvesting of this kind was practiced in inland Southern California from the 1890s into the 1920s, so the existing c. 1900–1930 range is retained; the print itself is undated.

img_a7a6b112d9c297dd.title: Studio portrait of Luis Moncada Estrada (1894–1980) as a young man
img_a7a6b112d9c297dd.description: A sepia studio bust portrait of a young man with side-parted hair and a mustache, in a suit with white shirt, striped tie, tie bar, and a small floral spray at the breast pocket — a rephotographed family print. He is Luis Moncada Estrada (1894–1980), who worked as a Southern Pacific track laborer from 1913 to 1947 on the Colton–Indio run through the San Gorgonio Pass, rose to section foreman, and with his wife Emeteria Lira raised ten children, moving the family to Beaumont in 1931, where they lived in an SP section house. He was honored posthumously: Beaumont named Luis Estrada Road for him (the BLD folder's '20 years' 2021 photo implies a 2001 naming), and in 2005 the California State Railroad Museum created a life-size figure of him driving a spike for exhibition. His attire and apparent age of roughly 25–35 fit the existing c. 1915–1930 range, which is retained.

img_31bfa277fbd3230d.description: Mounted album print captioned below in period ink 'Beaumont school house.' img_d6de78f86c47985e.description: A photograph of a newspaper page from the Community Advisor of November 12, 1987, whose 'A Glimpse Into…' feature runs a year-by-year Beaumont history timeline (entries visible for 'About 1820,' 1842, 'Before 1859,' and 1885) marking the 75th anniversary of the city's November 1912 incorporation — adjacent copy mentions 'Commemoration of the actual incorporation date.' McCoy, and laborer Ralph McCoy), and Holmes' 1912 county history records that J. J. McCoy built a house for his uncle, Judge McCoy, in 1884 and was chosen first president of Beaumont's board of trustees when the incorporation vote carried on November 6, 1912. The record's 1987 date belongs to the newspaper page; the underlying house photograph is undated.

img_7b302ec1a5a6c157.title: Reznor P. Stewart, Founder of the Stewart Ranch, Late-Life Snapshot, c. 1910-1933
img_7b302ec1a5a6c157.description: An elderly man with a full white beard, wearing a broad-brimmed hat and a vest over a work shirt, stands behind a wire fence in front of a ranch house, with garden flowers at lower right — a small amateur snapshot, unannotated and low-resolution in this copy. He is Reznor P. Stewart (c. 1845-1933), who homesteaded at Beaumont in 1883 and, buying additional Southern Pacific railroad land, built the Stewart Ranch to more than 2,200 acres of grain and hay; a 1974 obituary of his daughter calls him 'the first grain farmer in the area,' and he was a founder and long-time president of the Beaumont Bank (built 1911 as the Funk Building). He died in November 1933 at age 88 — a San Bernardino Sun item of 13 Nov 1933 describes 'Reznor P. Stewart, 88 years old and prominent in affairs...', and Notices to Creditors for his estate (No. 6530, with Laura M. Stewart as special administrator) ran in the Beaumont Daily Gazette from January 1934. His evident old age places the snapshot in roughly his last two decades, not the catalog's former 1900-1915 range. In 1962 Beaumont's cemetery was renamed Stewart Sunny Slope Cemetery in his family's honor.
